The interpreter told me an order on the proclamation of a Serbian Chetnik vojvoda. I don't know how it sounds in French. It's not an order. It's an instruction. It is a legal act which can be of an individual and a general nature. And in the classification of legal acts in the administration, for example, a "naredba" comes below the Statute and the Rules. If the Constitution is at the top, then comes a decree, and then at a lower level there is the Statute, the Rules, the ordinance or injection. There's something known as autonomous law of religious organisations, political parties, and so on, and this autonomous law contains elements of administrative law. So "naredba" is a legal act, an injunction, and not an order. An order exists in this sphere of command. Somebody gave somebody else an order to capture a bunker, this is not an order, it is an induction to proclaim somebody a vojvoda, whoever has the right to do this, on the basis of the Statute of the Serbian Radical Party, to proclaim a group of people as Serb Chetnik vojvodas. This may be purely a translation problem, but I thought it necessary to draw your attention to it. Substantially, however, let us for a moment put aside the fact that I think Slavko Aleksic is absolutely right in saying all this. I would say something like this and have said similar things. Now, what does this mean, producing Slavko Aleksic's statement from 1997 [Realtime transcript read as "1987"] as evidence in a case against me? If, in 1993, I proclaimed somebody a Chetnik vojvoda, does that mean that I bear responsibility for everything he did before he was proclaimed a Chetnik vojvoda and what he did after he was proclaimed a Chetnik vojvoda? He is not stupid, he's not a minor, I'm not his nurse. What do I care as to what someone said somewhere? I know why proclaimed him a Chetnik vojvoda; for his heroism during the war, for his courage, for his knightly behaviour. I didn't push him like a sheep somewhere who would listen to me and do whatever I say. So if he does something wrong, it is my fault as though he was an ultimatum that I was commanding. What does that mean, that every president of a political party in France would be responsible for anything any single member of that party does anywhere? Party members are arrested for a crime, they go to prison, and nobody charges the president of the party for this. He may be responsible politically. Where are the consequences in terms of criminal responsibility for something that somebody said outside of the period of the indictment? So I think perhaps the Prosecution should explain this. Perhaps the Trial Chamber understands this better than me. I seem to be the only one who doesn't understand anything here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing. There's an error on line 18, page 49. It's not "1987," but "1997." Very well. The Trial Chamber is going to confer as to whether we will or not admit this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unanimously, the Trial Chamber decides to admit this exhibit, and is thus asking Madam Registrar to give us a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will become Exhibit number P398, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. I believe, Mr. Prosecutor, that all videos were shown and played. Mr. Mussemeyer, I'd like to know, we saw all the videos; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we saw them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I would like to ask something to Mr. Mundis. In the future, will we have other videos? Are we going to see another list of videos?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We're working on that, Mr. President, and we'll be in a position to notify the Trial Chamber when we return on, I believe, the 6th of May. We should have some further information on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Very well. So next week, we are not sitting, because Wednesday is a day off and there will be no sitting next week, so we will resume on May 6, on Tuesday, May 6. I mentioned this yesterday. A witness has been scheduled for that day. It's still going on? Are there any problems expected?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: As of today, it's still going on, Mr. President. We are in possession of no information that would indicate that the witness scheduled, VS-002, will not appear. As far as we know, he is scheduled and will be here to testify from the 6th through the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you know that to govern this is to anticipate, and so if there is a problem, the Trial Chamber would like you to tell the senior legal officer as quickly as possible, as well as Mr. Seselj, to have something as a backup prepared, maybe another witness. But Mr. Seselj must be told about it in due time. The Trial Chamber had decided to have a court witness the week after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Obviously, if something happens with respect to the expected appearance of Witness VS-002, as long as we have enough advanced notice that that witness is not coming, we will schedule someone else. If we only find out the day or so before that witness is to come, that he is not going to appear, then we will certainly have problems in terms of getting witnesses here. As the Trial Chamber is well aware, VWS and the host state require five working days in order to process visas, and if we don't have at least five days to work with, then it's impossible to schedule witnesses that require visas, and that's the majority of the witnesses we're dealing with. So we will, of course, do our best, but as I've indicated, at this point in time we have no information or anything that would lead us to believe that we would have a problem with respect to the appearance of the witness scheduled for the 6th through the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Regarding Witness VS-002, I think you asked for four hours. That's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that we'd asked for three hours, but I'm not certain. I'm looking at the court calender that we distribute, and that indicates three hours. I certainly don't expect that we would have a problem with filling that whole week with the testimony of that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have three hours. Mr. Seselj will also be given three hours. But out of experience, we know that it takes much longer because of the different issues that are raised. So with three hours, I'm sure -- for three hours for each party, I'm sure we will have enough matter for three days. Mr. Mundis, is there anything you'd like to talk about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, do you have any topic you'd like to raise?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I filed two submissions -- three submissions today; the one you suggested yesterday regarding Carla Del Ponte, an amendment to the criminal report against an investigator of the OTP because of certain circumstances, and also a response to the request of the Prosecution for a change in the list of witnesses, and this is something that I have to elaborate on orally here. The Prosecution has renounced three witnesses. That is not a problem, as one of them has been on the Defence list for a long time now. But the Prosecution wants to include a new witness under 92 ter, and I resolutely object. First of all, he's belatedly being introduced, and, secondly, under 92 ter, I think it's not a protected witness, so I can use his name -- it is a woman, and if the OTP doesn't let me know that she is a protected witness, I can proceed. We're talking about Vesna Bosanac. I don't mind her being a witness, but if she comes here, then she has to be heard viva voce and in no other way, because this is a witness of capital importance for these proceedings. And the fact that the Prosecution is renouncing Ivan Grujic is a problem, because he has been compromised by his behaviour in the Glavas case, and they are now offering two other persons as experts instead of him. And I have elaborated on this objection in detail in my submission. I have been preparing for five years for Ivan Grujic. I spent a lot of money preparing to disqualify him as a man and as an expert, and now they, one or two of his associates, upon the suggestion of the Croatian government, to take over his role in these proceedings. And the Prosecution tells us that it is upon the suggestion of the Croatian government, and I find that absolutely unacceptable. And, finally, I ask the Trial Chamber to give instructions to the OTP to give to the Chamber and me a final list of remaining Prosecution witnesses, because I am finding it more and more difficult to find my way on that list, because the Prosecution has renounced some of them more recently and also there's quite a number of deceased witnesses. I'm not sure that the Prosecution knows that they have passed away. According to my records, there are eight or nine of them who have died in the meantime, and the Prosecution should clear these things up because they have time at their disposal, and to provide us a final text of -- list of remaining witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis, regarding the last part of Mr. Seselj's intervention regarding this updated witness list, I believe this is very appropriate, and it would be good if the Trial Chamber and Mr. Seselj were given an updated list. Now, Mr. Seselj is telling us that according to his own information, eight or nine witnesses scheduled on the original list are deceased. That's quite a large number of people, and this will have repercussions on the witness list. The Trial Chamber must absolutely know where it's going in order to know where you're going with your own witnesses, and it would be good to have an updated list with live witnesses, the ones that are still alive. If some witnesses passed away, I'm sure you know that the Rule 92 ter quater has been set up through which you may ask for the statements to be admitted in such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We are in the process of preparing a 92 quater motion covering a number of witnesses who have passed away since our witness list was created. I'm also meeting with members of the trial team tomorrow in order to put together a plan that will take us significantly farther down the road in terms of witness appearances and witness schedules. So I would anticipate that, again, when we return on the 6th of May, that we should be in a position to provide some further information. I will indicate that with the exception of any witnesses that the Prosecution has specifically withdrawn from its witness list, all of the witnesses on the original witness list remain on the Prosecution's witness list. So it's not going to be a situation where I come in on Monday and indicate that 45 witnesses on the Prosecution's list are being dropped. The only witnesses that we're not going to call are those witnesses that we have made written or oral applications concerning. All of the remaining witnesses remain on the Prosecution witness list. We are, as I've indicated, working to put together a scheduled plan that will take us many months down the road, and we are in the processing and filing and putting together a 92 quater motion that will take us a little bit of time in order to ensure that we've got all the proper material that needs to go with that filing. So I will probably be in a position to indicate further the exact status or plan that the Prosecution is putting forward to move forward, but I will again indicate that all of the witnesses on the Prosecution witness list remain on the Prosecution witness list unless we have specifically indicated otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, very well. Regarding Grujic, the expert witness, you told us that you had been preparing for him for years and that you believed it was quite abnormal that he should no longer be on the list. Now, regarding this issue, remember that each party controls its witnesses and establishes its own witness list, is envisaging that they will be heard, and sometimes there are exceptional circumstances that force parties to drop witnesses off their lists for different reasons. As an example, the Prosecutor could very well decide to drop witnesses that you're claiming as Defence witnesses. He is allowed to do that, just as he's allowed, if he decides to change expert witness, to explain why he wants to change the expert witness. Here, for example, a reason was given because he's been -- he's involved in a special case, and because of this, they would like to replace him with two other experts. Of course, the Trial Chamber will rule on this, but they're free to do this, just like you might be. At one point in time, you might want to call witnesses, and at the very last minute you could drop a scheduled witness for a reason that is your own, and the Prosecution can't say, "Well, I prepared for the cross-examination of Mr. Seselj's witness for years, and suddenly he's dropped off the list." That's the way things are organised under this procedure. You can think what you want about it, but that is the way things stand. The Prosecution controls its choice of witnesses and controls whether it wants the witnesses to be heard or not. Of course, the Prosecution has this authority, but the Trial Chamber can decide that in the interest of justice, even if the witness is dropped from the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber may want this witness to come anyway. That's up to the Chamber to decide, just like if a witness is dropped from the Prosecution list, the Defence can call this witness if Defence wishes to do that. That's the way it works.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I consider that this problem is far more complicated than that. I completely agree that the Prosecutor can withdraw any of his witnesses, but here we're not talking with dropping a witness and we're not dealing with dropping an expert witness. What we're talking about here is to replace an expert witness, and I think that in previous trials we haven't come across a case like that, or at least I don't know about it. And the OTP therefore recognises that this particular witness has been discredited, which entails enormous repercussions. He testified in the Milosevic trial, the Vukovar Trojka trial, and who knows in what other trial. And if he's been discredited as an expert witness, then his expert testimony must be dropped in all those trials. The second problem is this: They say, "The expert witness has been disqualified, so we're not going to call him but we're going to call his associates from his -- the same institution that he works with -- that he worked with together," so that they could instead of him explain and interpret what he had prepared to put to the Trial Chamber. And even more that; that this was done pursuant to suggestions of the Croatian government, the Croatian government suggested that, the authorities in Croatia stated that, that they take these two women to testify instead of Ivan Grujic. I can't remember their names, but it's in my written statement. So that they should do that instead of him. So it's material prepared by Ivan Grujic, and let me remind you then that we never actually had a true expert report, it was just a collection of different material, and now instead of him -- and I said that I would challenge everything he said, that I would challenge his credibility as a witness, his professionalism, and so on and so forth. We now have the appearance of two other people, two women, to interpret all this, and they probably worked on this matter with him. They're probably not incompetent, but I think that in my deep opinion, that the -- this action is not in order, that somebody should be dropped because the Prosecution concluded that he has lost credibility. Instead of him, two associates, pursuant to suggestions from the Croatian government were called instead of him to interpret the material that he compiled and created and collected or did whatever he did himself. So that's the crux of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your problem was explained -- rather, you've explained it to us. The Chamber will rule on this. The submissions were presented orally and in writing. And the last point that you raised, which is the changing of the list by adding a witness that will testify on the Vukovar Hospital, it is a lady. She's already testified previously. She made a written statement, and there's a request to add her. You were able to make your comments, and the Trial Chamber will decide on this. All the topics were dealt with, and since we have some time and had some time, it was good that we were able to deal with this, and now we are going to be able in the future to devote our time to witnesses. We won't be -- it won't be needed to talk about administrative questions or housekeeping matters. We can just focus on the witnesses. And since today we had some time, it was important and useful to deal with these matters. Unless I am mistaken, Mr. Seselj, you talked about all the topics you wished to raise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This being said, the hearing is resumed [sic] and we will -- the hearing is adjourned, rather, and we will resume the hearing on the 6th of May. Thank you very much.
